lead: A random variable assigns a real number to each outcome of an experiment, such as a noise voltage sampled at one instant or the number of bit errors in a packet. Its distribution gives the probability that the number falls in any range. A receiver compares noisy samples with a threshold, so these tools predict its error rate. This chapter reviews probability rules, random variables and their moments, the common distributions, and functions of random variables.
prereq: You need: sets, sums and integrals; no earlier chapter of this book.

sections.h3: Probability rules, conditioning and Bayes' rule

blocks.text: An experiment has a sample space S, the set of all outcomes. An event A is a subset of S. Probability obeys three axioms: P(A) ≥ 0; P(S) = 1; and for disjoint events, P(A1 ∪ A2 ∪ …) = P(A1) + P(A2) + …. From them follow P(Ac) = 1 − P(A) and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

blocks.where: P(A|B) is the probability of A given that B occurred; it is defined only when P(B) > 0.

blocks.text: Rearranged, it gives the multiplication rule P(A ∩ B) = P(A|B)P(B). Events A and B are independent when P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B); then, if P(B) > 0, P(A|B) = P(A). Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so two exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are never independent.

If A1, …, An split S into disjoint pieces, the total probability of B is P(B) = Σ P(B|Ai)P(Ai), and Bayes' rule reverses the condition: P(Ai|B) = P(B|Ai)P(Ai) / P(B). In a receiver Ai is "symbol i was sent" (the prior), B is what was received, P(B|Ai) is the likelihood and P(Ai|B) the posterior. Worked example 2 uses it on a binary channel.

sections.h3: Random variables, CDF, PDF and moments

blocks.text: A random variable X maps each outcome to a real number. Its cumulative distribution function (CDF) is FX(x) = P(X ≤ x): it never decreases, is right-continuous, and runs from FX(−∞) = 0 to FX(∞) = 1. A discrete variable has a probability mass function pX(x) = P(X = x). A continuous variable has a probability density function (PDF) fX(x) = dFX/dx, with total area 1 and P(a < X ≤ b) = FX(b) − FX(a) = ∫ fX(x) dx from a to b. The height fX(x) is a density, not a probability, and P(X = x) = 0 for every single x.

The mean is μ = E[X] = ∫ x fX(x) dx (or Σ x pX(x)). The variance is σ² = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − μ², and σ is the standard deviation, in the units of X. E[X²] is the mean-square value: for a noise voltage it is the average power in 1 Ω, and it equals σ² only when μ = 0. A linear change Y = aX + b gives E[Y] = aμ + b and var(Y) = a²σ².

blocks.text: For the standard Gaussian (μ = 0, σ = 1), Φ(z) = P(Z ≤ z) and the tail is Q(z) = P(Z > z) = 1 − Φ(z). Useful values: Q(1) = 0.1587, Q(2) = 0.0228, Q(3) = 0.00135. A Gaussian X is turned into Z by z = (x − μ)/σ. When n is large and p small, the binomial is close to a Poisson with λ = np.

sections.h3: Joint variables, functions of a variable and the CLT

blocks.text: Two variables have a joint PDF fXY(x, y). The marginal is fX(x) = ∫ fXY(x, y) dy and the conditional is fX|Y(x|y) = fXY(x, y)/fY(y) where fY(y) > 0. X and Y are independent when fXY = fXfY, and uncorrelated when E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]. Independence implies uncorrelated, but not the reverse; only for jointly Gaussian variables does zero correlation imply independence.

For a function Y = g(X) that is monotonic and differentiable, fY(y) = fX(x)/|g′(x)| with x = g−1(y); if several x give the same y, add the term for each root. The CDF method, FY(y) = P(g(X) ≤ y) and then differentiate, always works. Some syllabi call this transformation of random variables. The characteristic function φX(ω) = E[ejωX] is the Fourier transform of the PDF with the sign of the exponent reversed, and its derivatives at ω = 0 give the moments.

The central limit theorem (CLT): the sum of n independent, identically distributed variables with finite variance tends to a Gaussian as n grows, with mean and variance equal to the sums of the means and variances. For terms that are not identical, an extra condition (Lindeberg's) must keep any one term from dominating. Thermal noise, a sum of countless tiny electron contributions, is therefore Gaussian.

examples.question: A Gaussian noise voltage V has mean 0 mV and standard deviation 2 mV. Find the probability that a sample exceeds 4 mV, and the probability that it lies between −2 mV and 2 mV.
steps: Standardize the threshold: z = (4 − 0)/2 = 2.0, a pure number (standard deviations).
P(V > 4 mV) = Q(2) = 0.0228, about 2.3 %. Because V is continuous, P(V ≥ 4 mV) is the same number.
For the band: z<sub>1</sub> = (−2 − 0)/2 = −1 and z<sub>2</sub> = (2 − 0)/2 = 1.
Check: by symmetry 1 − 2(0.0228) = 0.9545 of samples lie within ±4 mV, the familiar two-sigma figure.

examples.question: A binary channel carries 1s with probability 0.6 and 0s with probability 0.4. A sent 1 is received as 0 with probability 0.05; a sent 0 is received as 1 with probability 0.1. Find the probability that a 1 is received, the probability that a 1 was sent given that a 1 is received, and the overall error probability.

traps: A PDF can be taller than 1; only an area is a probability, and P(X = x) = 0 for a continuous X.
For non-zero mean, E[X²] = σ² + μ², not σ². Variance is in units squared; the standard deviation is in the units of X.
P(A|B) and P(B|A) are different numbers: 0.934 and 0.95 in worked example 2. Bayes' rule is the bridge between them.
In the Gaussian exponent use σ², and standardize with z = (x − μ)/σ. Q(z) is the upper tail and Φ(z) the lower area; do not mix them.
Uncorrelated does not mean independent, except for jointly Gaussian variables. Exclusive is not the same as independent.

quiz.q: State the three axioms of probability.
quiz.a: P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A; P(S) = 1; for disjoint events P(A<sub>1</sub> ∪ A<sub>2</sub> ∪ …) = P(A<sub>1</sub>) + P(A<sub>2</sub>) + ….

quiz.q: Why can a PDF have height 2 while a probability is never above 1?
quiz.a: The height is a density per unit x. Probability is the area over an interval. A uniform PDF on [0, 0.5] has height 2, but its total area is 2 × 0.5 = 1.

quiz.q: In 1000 bits with bit error probability 0.002, find the mean number of errors and the probability of no error (Poisson approximation).
quiz.a: λ = np = 2, so P(0) = e<sup>−2</sup> = 0.135 (the exact binomial 0.998<sup>1000</sup> is also 0.135).

quiz.q: How does Bayes' rule combine prior and likelihood in a bit detector?
quiz.a: P(1|v) = f(v|1)P(1) / [f(v|1)P(1) + f(v|0)P(0)]. The prior P(1) is weighted by the likelihood f(v|1) of the received voltage v, and the denominator is the total probability of v.

quiz.q: Does zero correlation imply independence? Give a counterexample.
quiz.a: No. Let X be uniform on [−1, 1] and Y = X². Then E[XY] = E[X³] = 0 = E[X]E[Y], so they are uncorrelated, yet Y is fixed by X. Zero correlation implies independence only when X and Y are jointly Gaussian.

quiz.q: A noise voltage is Gaussian with σ = 1 mV. A detector declares a pulse when the voltage exceeds 3 mV. With no pulse present, how often does it raise a false alarm, and how does halving σ change this?
quiz.a: z = 3/1 = 3, so P = Q(3) = 0.00135, about 1 in 740 samples. With σ = 0.5 mV, z = 6 and Q(6) ≈ 1×10<sup>−9</sup>: halving the noise makes false alarms about a million times rarer.

quiz.q: State the central limit theorem and one use in communication.
quiz.a: The sum of many independent, identically distributed variables with finite variance tends to a Gaussian with mean and variance equal to the sums of the means and variances. It justifies the Gaussian model of thermal noise.

beyond: Not for the exam. Link budgets use the Q function to turn a noise standard deviation into a bit error rate, and fading channels use the Rayleigh and Rician laws met here. Search for Q function table and Rician fading to go further.
